title: `ia author` applies previewed permitted record edits with digest checks
summary: @inventarch/cli adds `ia author` (catalog row: mode author, move Synthesis) for permitted record words. It accepts the corresponding preview arguments and --digest <sha256>, the target file digest printed by the preview. It compiles the candidate again against one editor snapshot, applies the author-mode mandate profile, and writes only when the digest still identifies the current file and the candidate is clean. Existing files use an opened-handle recheck and guarded temporary-file replacement; new files use create-only publication. The edit preserves surrounding records, line endings, a byte-order mark and existing permission bits. One attribution comment records the acting participant, a governing mandate granting Synthesis and the authored revision; a later author replaces that comment rather than stacking it. Attribution and --actor are local declarations, not authentication. The final integrated source-protection boundary refuses author mutations of workspace, agent, mandate, system, schema, agent-profile and hook records for every actor, including an ungoverned actor. This covers creation, field edits and relationship edits, so `ia author system` does not write a starter system and changing actors does not bypass this administrative-word boundary. Existing profile, ownership and binding-mandate refusals keep precedence. Previews remain read-only; direct owner source edits followed by validation remain the administrative path. The separate administrative-authoring note describes this breaking boundary and doctor warnings. Every successful author command names a profile-judged next command. Refusals retain preview's diagnostics, plus missing or malformed --digest (IA-CLI-USAGE, exit 2), changed input (IA-CLI-EDIT-STALE, exit 1), an unclean candidate (IA-CLI-EDIT-UNCLEAN, exit 1), and distribution or volume failures (exit 3). A refusal writes nothing. One record, row or field is written per invocation, and `ia author` does not execute operations. Mandates and these CLI refusals are cooperative restrictions, not filesystem isolation: a direct file edit remains possible, and a source-protection declaration alone does not prove that a host enforces it.
